title: Why would you use a Schema Registry instead of just sending JSON?
shortTitle: Why use a Schema Registry instead of just sending JSON

s1_definition.profdef: A Schema Registry is a centralized service that stores and versions the schemas describing the structure of the messages on each Kafka topic, and it enforces compatibility rules when schemas evolve. Producers serialize data using a registered schema, typically Avro, Protobuf, or JSON Schema, and the message carries only a compact schema id rather than the full field definitions; consumers fetch the matching schema by id to deserialize. Compared with sending raw JSON, a Schema Registry gives you enforced, versioned, backward- and forward-compatible contracts between producers and consumers, smaller payloads, and automatic rejection of messages that would break downstream consumers.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India sends transfer forms between departments. Sending plain JSON is like letting every clerk write the form freehand — one writes "amt", another writes "amount", someone forgets the currency, and the receiving department silently misreads it. A Schema Registry is like the bank publishing an official, numbered form template that everyone must use, with rules that any new version of the form must still be readable by departments using the old version. Every form just references the template number instead of reprinting the whole template, saving paper, and the mailroom refuses any form that does not match an approved template.
s1_definition.oneliner: A Schema Registry enforces versioned, compatible message contracts and shrinks payloads, whereas raw JSON leaves the contract unwritten and unprotected.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Schema Registry is a centralized service that stores and versions the schemas describing the structure of the messages on each Kafka topic, and it enforces compatibility rules when schemas evolve. Producers serialize data using a registered schema, typically Avro, Protobuf, or JSON Schema, and the message carries only a compact schema id rather than the full field definitions; consumers fetch the matching schema by id to deserialize. Compared with sending raw JSON, a Schema Registry gives you enforced, versioned, backward- and forward-compatible contracts between producers and consumers, smaller payloads, and automatic rejection of messages that would break downstream consumers.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India sends transfer forms between departments. Sending plain JSON is like letting every clerk write the form freehand — one writes "amt", another writes "amount", someone forgets the currency, and the receiving department silently misreads it. A Schema Registry is like the bank publishing an official, numbered form template that everyone must use, with rules that any new version of the form must still be readable by departments using the old version. Every form just references the template number instead of reprinting the whole template, saving paper, and the mailroom refuses any form that does not match an approved template.

**One line to remember:** A Schema Registry enforces versioned, compatible message contracts and shrinks payloads, whereas raw JSON leaves the contract unwritten and unprotected.

sections.s2_technical:
The central problem with sending raw JSON is that there is no enforced contract. JSON is self-describing but schemaless from Kafka's point of view — the producer can add, rename, remove, or retype fields at any time, and Kafka happily carries whatever bytes it is given. A consumer written to expect a field called amount as a number may suddenly receive amt as a string, or a missing field, and it breaks at runtime, often in production, with no warning at deploy time. In a bank, a silently misread amount or currency is a serious incident.

A Schema Registry solves this by making the schema a first-class, versioned artifact. When a producer sends a record, the serializer registers or looks up the schema in the registry and gets back a numeric schema id. The message on the wire is the schema id plus the compactly encoded data. The consumer's deserializer reads the id, fetches the exact schema from the registry (caching it), and decodes the data reliably. Both sides now agree on structure by construction. In Spring you configure this with a value serializer like KafkaAvroSerializer and a `schema.registry.url`.

The second major benefit is controlled schema evolution with compatibility checks. The registry enforces a configured compatibility mode when a new schema version is registered. Backward compatibility means new consumers can read data written with the old schema, typically achieved by only adding fields with defaults. Forward compatibility means old consumers can read data written by a new schema. Full compatibility means both. If a producer team tries to register a change that would break the rule — for example removing a required field or changing a type — the registry rejects the registration, so the breaking change is caught at deploy time, not discovered by a crashing consumer in production. This lets a large bank evolve its event formats safely across dozens of independently deployed services.

The third benefit is payload efficiency. With Avro or Protobuf plus a schema id, the message does not repeat field names in every record the way JSON does; it carries compact binary data and a small id. Over millions of transaction events, this significantly reduces network bandwidth and storage. JSON, by contrast, repeats every key name in every message, which is wasteful at scale.

There are trade-offs to acknowledge. The registry is another service to run and make highly available, and it adds a small lookup on first use of each schema, though schemas are cached. JSON is simpler for small systems, human-readable, and easy to debug by eye. You can even use JSON Schema inside the registry to keep readability while gaining enforcement. The senior-level nuance is that for a large, multi-team, money-handling system, the cost of an unenforced contract — a consumer silently misreading a transfer amount, or a breaking change shipped to production — far outweighs the operational cost of running a registry. So the decision is about scale and risk: raw JSON is acceptable for a tiny internal tool, but for a banking event backbone with many producers and consumers evolving independently, a Schema Registry with a strict compatibility mode is the professional default. It turns the message format into a governed, versioned API contract rather than an informal convention.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India had a production incident where a producer team renamed a field and several consumer services broke, and the team now wants enforced, versioned message contracts.

Problem 1 — Different teams interpreted the transfer message differently — one expected amount, another amt — and consumers broke when the producer changed a field. This is exactly what a Schema Registry prevents by enforcing one agreed, registered schema.

Problem 2 — When the bank needed to add a new currency field, it had to be sure existing consumers would not break. This is exactly backward-compatible schema evolution — add the field with a default so old consumers still read new messages.

Problem 3 — A producer team once tried to remove a required field, which would have broken live consumers. This is exactly the registry's compatibility check rejecting the breaking change at deploy time.

The mini-project simulates a schema registry. We build a `Schema` with a version and fields, a `SchemaRegistry` that registers schemas under a subject and enforces backward compatibility, a `AvroLikeSerializer` that encodes a message as a schema id plus data, and a `Consumer` that deserializes by fetching the schema by id. The demo registers version one, evolves to version two by adding a field with a default (accepted), then attempts an incompatible change (rejected), and shows a consumer safely decoding both versions.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is a sequence of schema registrations for the transfers-value subject and one transfer message serialized with the latest accepted schema.

Step 1 — Version one of the transfer schema is registered with fields transferId, fromAccount, toAccount, and amount. Since there is no prior version, it is accepted and assigned schema id one. This is now the agreed contract.

Step 2 — Version two adds a currency field while keeping all four original fields. The registry checks backward compatibility: because version two still contains every field of version one, old consumers can still read it, so it is accepted and assigned schema id two. The format evolved safely.

Step 3 — A third schema attempts to remove the required amount field. The registry checks it against the latest version and sees that it no longer contains the amount field, which would break existing consumers. The registration is rejected at this point, before any such message is ever produced. The breaking change is caught at deploy time, not in production.

Step 4 — The producer serializes a transfer using schema id two. The wire message is the schema id followed by the compact values, without repeating field names like JSON would. This is smaller than the equivalent JSON.

Step 5 — The consumer reads the wire message, extracts the schema id, fetches the exact schema from the registry, and decodes the values into the correct fields reliably. There is no guessing about field names or types. The logs show version one accepted, version two accepted as compatible, the breaking change rejected, and a message serialized and deserialized through the enforced contract.

```
2026-10-24 20:42:00 [INFO] REGISTERED transfers-value v1[transferId, fromAccount, toAccount, amount] as id=1
2026-10-24 20:42:00 [INFO] REGISTERED transfers-value v2[transferId, fromAccount, toAccount, amount, currency] as id=2
2026-10-24 20:42:00 [SEVERE] REJECT transfers-value v3[transferId, fromAccount, toAccount] — not backward compatible with v2[transferId, fromAccount, toAccount, amount, currency] (would break existing consumers)
2026-10-24 20:42:00 [INFO] SERIALIZE with schema id=2 -> wire=2|TXF-1,SAV2001,CUR3001,50000,INR, (field names NOT repeated on the wire)
2026-10-24 20:42:00 [INFO] DESERIALIZE using schema id=2 -> {transferId=TXF-1, fromAccount=SAV2001, toAccount=CUR3001, amount=50000, currency=INR} (reliable, contract enforced)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Producer                              Schema Registry                 Consumer
  ──────────                            ────────────────                ─────────
  data {transferId, from, to,            register(subject, schema)
        amount, currency}                 ├─ v1 → id=1 (accepted)
    │ get schema id                       ├─ v2 (+currency default) → id=2 (compatible)
    │                                     └─ v3 (-amount) → REJECTED (breaks consumers)
    ▼                                            ▲ lookup by id
  serialize → [id=2 | compact values] ──────────┼──────────────────────────┐
    │  (NO field names repeated, small)          │                          ▼
    ▼                                             │               fetch schema id=2
  Kafka topic transfers ──────────────────────────┘               decode reliably
                                                                   {amount=50000, currency=INR}

  vs RAW JSON: {"amount":50000,...} every key repeated, NO contract, NO compat check,
  a renamed/removed field silently breaks consumers at runtime.
```

```
  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐

  │ O: new compatibility rule = new check, callers unchanged     │

  │ + getById(id): Schema         │

          │ uses          │ uses
          ▼               ▼
  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐
  │ AvroLikeSerializer│  │ TransferConsumer │
  │ + serialize(...)  │  │ + consume(wire)  │
  │   [id|values]     │  │   fetch by id    │
  └──────────────────┘  └──────────────────┘
                 │ describes
                 ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │            Schema             │
  │ - version: int                │
  │ - fields: Set<String>         │
  │ + isBackwardCompatibleWith(s) │
  └──────────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: a schema version ───────────────────────────

  [PROPOSED] → compatible with latest? 
      ├─ yes → [REGISTERED (new version, new id)]
      └─ no  → [REJECTED] (breaking change blocked)

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────────

  1. registry.register("transfers-value", v1) → id=1
  2. registry.register(..., v2 +currency) → compatible → id=2
  3. registry.register(..., v3 -amount) → REJECT
  4. serializer.serialize(subject, id=2, data) → [2|values]
  5. consumer.consume(wire) → getById(2) → decode reliably

  Contract for register(subject, schema):
    Pre:  schema non-null
    Post: id assigned ONLY if compatible with latest version
    Rule: reject breaking changes before any message is produced
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
I would use a Schema Registry instead of raw JSON because it turns the message format into a governed, versioned contract between producers and consumers, which raw JSON cannot provide. The core problem with sending plain JSON is that there is no enforced schema — the producer can add, rename, remove, or retype a field at any time, and Kafka carries whatever bytes it is given. A consumer expecting a numeric amount might suddenly get a string, a renamed field, or a missing field, and it breaks at runtime in production. In a bank, a silently misread transfer amount or currency is a serious incident.

A Schema Registry makes the schema a first-class, versioned artifact. The producer serializes with a registered schema, usually Avro or Protobuf, and the message on the wire carries a compact schema id plus binary data rather than repeating field names. The consumer reads the id, fetches the exact schema, and decodes reliably, so both sides agree on structure by construction. On top of that, the registry enforces a compatibility mode when a new schema version is registered — backward compatibility lets new consumers read old data, forward lets old consumers read new data, and full gives both. If a team tries to register a breaking change, like removing a required field, the registry rejects it at deploy time instead of letting a consumer crash in production.

There is also a real efficiency gain. Avro or Protobuf with a schema id carries compact binary data and a small id, while JSON repeats every key name in every message, which is wasteful across millions of transaction events. I do acknowledge the trade-offs honestly — the registry is another service to run and keep highly available, and JSON is simpler and human-readable for small systems. You can even use JSON Schema inside the registry to keep readability while gaining enforcement.

In my banking platform at National Bank of India, we adopted a Schema Registry after a production incident where a producer team renamed a field and several consumers broke. Now every transfer topic has a registered schema with backward compatibility enforced, so when we added a currency field we gave it a default and old consumers kept working, and an attempt to remove a required field was rejected before it ever shipped. The senior point I make is that this is a decision about scale and risk: raw JSON is fine for a tiny internal tool, but for a banking event backbone with many teams evolving independently, the cost of an unenforced contract far outweighs running a registry, so a Schema Registry with a strict compatibility mode is the professional default.
